entities.name: Adal Sultanate
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Adal Sultanate (c. 1415–1577 CE), based in Zeila and later Harar in the Horn of Africa, was the Islamic sultanate that conducted the most successful jihad in African history — Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi ('Ahmad Grañ' — 'the Left-Handed') conquered approximately 75% of the Ethiopian Empire between 1529-1543, nearly destroying Africa's oldest continuous Christian kingdom. The Portuguese military intervention under Cristóvão da Gama (son of Vasco da Gama) in 1541-1543 rescued Ethiopia from complete conquest — a collision of African Islam, Ethiopian Christianity, and Portuguese global exploration.

The Adal Sultanate emerged from the Ifat Sultanate's remnants after Ethiopian Emperor Yeshaq's campaigns. Ahmad Grañ, a brilliant military commander who adopted Ottoman firearms acquired through the Red Sea trade, used musket-armed infantry to defeat Ethiopia's traditional cavalry. Between 1529 and 1543, Ahmad Grañ's forces burned over half of Ethiopia's churches and monasteries, destroyed irreplaceable manuscripts, forced mass conversion to Islam, and reduced the empire to a highland remnant.

Portugal's intervention in 1541 — sending 400 musketeers under Cristóvão da Gama, who was captured and executed by Ahmad Grañ — was followed by a second campaign under Galawdewos that killed Ahmad Grañ in 1543, reversing most of his conquests. The Adal-Ethiopian war's 14 years nearly destroyed Ethiopian Christianity and permanently changed the Horn's demographic balance. The Oromo migrations (1550s-1600s) that followed the war's population devastation permanently reshaped Ethiopian and Somali ethnic geography.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Adal Sultanate's near-conquest of Ethiopia — reversed only by Portuguese military intervention — represents the closest Africa's oldest continuous Christian kingdom came to destruction, and the first collision of sub-Saharan African Christianity, African Islam, and European global expansion.
